text.en: Take this lichen, wrap it around some root vegetables like camas, and bake it in an earth oven for a few days. You'll get a delicious loaf with the consistency of licorice. That's what many First Nations in the BC Interior used to do. They also used it to make clothes and shoes. Researchers have found that the lichen absorbs nutrients from the vegetables that would otherwise be lost during cooking.

details.notes: Label reads: Wila (Secwepemc name) / Edible horsehair lichen / Bryoria fremontii. Photos show the lichen growing on a tree, and prepared as dark loaves (traditional food preparation). Small text on label partially illegible for catalog number.

text.en: Crustose lichens hang on tight, forming splotches of colour over trees, rocks, soil, old antlers, and anything else that stays still long enough. Foliose lichens are leaf-like, often hanging loose or attached by fur-like growths called rhizines. Fruticose lichens are truly three-dimensional. Some species look like tiny shrubs or hang in long strands.

details.notes: Large multi-section panel showing three lichen growth forms: Crustose, Foliose, and Fruticose, with labeled specimens in each category. 17 specimens total with catalog numbers.

text.en: All these mushrooms are edible: maybe you've even feasted on their unique tastes and textures. But did you know that hundreds of edible mushroom species grow here in British Columbia, from oyster mushrooms to morels? But it's easy to make a mistake identifying edible mushrooms, so never go mushroom hunting without an experienced guide. The poisonous ivory funnel mushroom looks like an oyster mushroom. Can you spot three differences between them?

details.notes: Upper section shows 8 edible mushroom specimens in a bordered display case. Lower section has comparison photos of ivory funnel vs oyster mushroom. Photo credit partially visible: Kent Brothers.

text.en: The most common fungal diseases are athlete's foot and ringworm, and they grow only on the surface of the skin, hair, or nails of mammals or the feathers of birds.

Two circular containers show feathers before (left, healthy golden-brown feathers) and after infection (below, degraded/damaged feathers). Caption: 'Feathers before (left) and after infection (below).' Lower text: 'Onychomycosis, or ringworm of the nail, can be caused by the fungus Trichophyton rubrum. It can take four months for the antifungal medicine to cure the disease.' Medicine bottle is from Shoppers Drug Mart: TERBINAFINE 250MG, 'Take ONE tablet(s) daily for 4 months.' text.en: Scientists have traditionally studied the lichen by looking at its component parts: the fungus plus the alga or cyanobacterium. But a new approach challenges lichenologists to think of the lichen as a complex, self-sustaining ecosystem—far more than the sum of its parts. Lichens contain producers (algae), consumers (fungi), and decomposers (fungi and bacteria), just like ecosystems.

Bottom section mentions Trevor Goward as curator of UBC's lichen collection and his role encouraging innovative thinking about lichens. Photo credit: University of British Columbia.

text.en: Fungi recycle wood, returning nutrients to soil. Hidden inside, they can digest wood until it crumbles. Later, fungi reveal themselves as shelf-like fruiting bodies — conks — that send out spores to infect more wood. Brown lignin remains after brown rot fungi digest cellulose from wood. White rot fungi remove brown lignin in wood, leaving white cellulose.

details.notes: Shows wood decomposition by fungi. Upper section contrasts brown rot (western hemlock, E.0079) and white rot (bigleaf maple, E.0080) wood samples, both collected June 21, 2010 from University Endowment Lands, Vancouver, BC. Lower section shows conk specimens: artist's conk cross-section (E.0078) and red-belt conk collection (E.0069–E.0076). Multiple small fungal fruiting bodies also visible along the curved display band. Catalog numbers corrected from previous extraction.

text.en: Heteroptera's 40,000-plus species worldwide include carnivores like the assassin bug, herbivores like the squash bug, and parasites like the infamous bed bug. Some of these "true bugs," such as water striders and back-swimmers, are aquatic.

details.notes: Overview display of Heteroptera (true bugs) organized by infraorder: Pentatomomorpha, Nepomorpha, Gerromorpha, Leptopodomorpha, Cimicomorpha. Multiple pinned specimens per family shown. No individual catalog numbers visible.

text.en: What makes a bug a true bug? The answer is that all true bugs have special mouthparts for piercing plants or other insects and sucking on their fluids. You might have seen these true bugs in your own backyard. The assassin bug paralyzes its prey by injecting it with toxic saliva.

details.notes: Includes electron microscope image of assassin bug mouthparts. Five labeled specimens with catalog numbers.

text.en: Is your turf all torn up? If birds and skunks are digging through your lawn looking for a tasty snack, your soil is probably infested with European chafer beetle grubs. The first BC sighting was in New Westminster in 2001. This invader is now common across the Lower Mainland. Tall, healthy lawns can fend off the grubs. Infestations can be controlled by applying predatory nematodes, available from large garden centres.

details.notes: Life cycle diagram of European chafer shown. Adult beetles and larvae displayed as specimens. Photo credit partially visible at bottom left.

text.en: Jumping spiders hunt like cats: when they spot prey with their big eyes, they sneak up and pounce. Females also use their big eyes to watch colourful males wooing them with elaborate dances.

details.notes: Multiple macro photographs of jumping spiders surround the specimens. All photos by Wayne Maddison. One specimen visible in a small container (bark/twig habitat).

text.en: Born in rivers, lakes, or ponds, caddisfly larvae are known as "underwater architects" because they build themselves protective cases out of things like gravel, twigs, sand, or other materials held together with strands of silk.

details.notes: Four caddisfly larval cases displayed with corresponding illustrations showing case architecture. Credit: Artiom Shostak visible at bottom. Small icons in circles show case cross-section patterns.

text.en: When you can't run, you hide -- we all know that from our days in the playground. Insects have figured that out too, which is why so many of them have evolved to blend into their surroundings in order to avoid getting eaten by birds and animals.

details.notes: Text-only panel about insect camouflage. No specimens visible. Label in corner reads S015, suggesting this may be a title/introductory panel for a camouflage-themed display. The file is named s095 but the visible label reads S015.

text.en: Like birds, some butterflies and moths make incredible voyages from breeding grounds to overwintering sites each year. Monarch butterflies, some flying a thousand metres above the ground, travel thousands of kilometres, from breeding sites in Canada and the northern United States to overwintering sites in Mexico and California. Each new generation of monarchs knows exactly where to find their ancestors' roosts.

details.notes: Includes photo of monarchs roosting in trees, credited to Beth Sargent. Specimen listed as from teaching collection with no catalog number.

text.en: Brilliant metallic colouring helps some butterflies confuse predators and communicate with each other. Instead of pigments, microscopic structures on their wings create these colours through interference — selectively cancelling out certain light wavelengths and reflecting others, in the same way as oil creates iridescent rainbows on water.

details.notes: Includes two SEM (scanning electron microscope) images of wing scale structures at upper right, labeled '100PM 10KV 05 003'. No species labels visible for any of the four butterfly specimens.

text.en: Some insects survive by disguising themselves as animals their predators avoid — a strategy called mimicry. For example, hoverflies scare off predators by mimicking the black and yellow stripes of wasps (such as a yellowjacket). Little do the predators know, the flies are harmless! Can you tell which of these insects are not dangerous and are sending a false warning? (Answers are hidden in the illustration above)

details.notes: Interactive quiz-style exhibit about insect mimicry. Split illustration shows hoverfly (left) vs yellowjacket (right). Specimens appear faded/washed out in photo. Five specimens labeled A through E.

text.en: "The Creator, if He exists, has an inordinate fondness for beetles." Attributed to J.B.S. Haldane

text.en: Goliath beetles, from Africa, are the heaviest insects in the world. The Atlas moth, of Southeast Asia, has the largest wingspan. In the past, insects were even bigger. Hold your arms out wide: that’s how big a dragonfly was when dinosaurs walked the earth!

text.en: People eat insects every day in many parts of the world. Grasshoppers, mealworms, giant water bugs, and ants are popular choices. Insects are high in protein and iron, low in fat, cheap to rear, and easy to prepare. Raising a cow costs astronomically more than producing the same amount of insect protein. Now there’s some food for thought!

details.notes: Includes photo of silkworm larvae for sale in Seoul, Korea (credit Derek Tan). Also shows commercial products: 'Larvets Original Worm Snax BBQ' package and an insect lollipop. Line drawing of various larvae/insects at lower right (credit Sigal Friedmann).

text.en: When a dead body is found, forensic entomologists use the insects associated with it to help discover when the person died. If a body is fresh, they’ll find mostly blow flies. But as the corpse ages, insects like house flies and carrion beetles multiply. To establish the time of death, these scientists need to understand insect development and be able to identify species.

details.notes: Forensic entomology theme. Illustration shows crime scene with three figures and 'POLICE LINE DO NOT CROSS' tape. No catalog numbers visible for any specimens. House flies labeled by family Muscidae rather than genus/species.

text.en: Carrion beetles love to eat carcasses: gross maybe, but essential work. Adult beetles are drawn to a body by the smell of decay. Only flies get there faster. Once the beetles arrive, they eat fly maggots and carrion, mate, and lay eggs. Carrion beetle larvae feed on fly maggots as well as the carcass, then burrow into the ground to pupate. Adult carrion beetles emerge from underground three weeks later to start the cycle again.

text.en: The buzz of bees might be hot gossip. Bees and wasps are social, living together and sharing the work. The queen lays eggs fertilized by male drones, and female workers build the nest and care for the young. Drones are short-lived: they die after mating. The cells of the comb house the young bees.

text.en: Sometimes the best way to control an invasive species is by introducing a predator — a strategy called biocontrol. Diffuse knapweed has been taking over the grasslands of the BC Interior for decades. Although 12 species of insect herbivores were introduced as biocontrol agents, only after the establishment of the weevil Larinus minutus did UBC scientists observe a dramatic decline in knapweed density. Judith Myers is a professor in UBC's Department of Zoology. She studies biocontrol and insect population cycles.

text.en: Beetles are the most diverse group of insects in the world. Look for these ground beetles, long-horned beetles, weevils, and ladybird beetles in your backyard or garden.

text.en: Most spiders live alone, but about two dozen known species of tropical spiders are social, living in large colonies. They cooperate in maintaining a communal web and caring for the colony's offspring. Working together, they can catch bigger prey than one spider could alone. Leticia Aviles is a professor in UBC's Department of Zoology. She has studied social spiders in Ecuador and Brazil to understand why organisms live in groups and cooperate.

text.en: If you've ever scratched a bug bite, you know how annoying (and painful!) biting flies can be. Deer flies, horse flies, black flies, mosquitoes, and many other biting flies use piercing mouthparts to feed on human and other animal blood.

details.notes: Illustrative/diagrammatic display only. Purple line drawings show mouthpart anatomy and cross-sections of skin penetration for each fly type. Three magnifier lenses mounted on display (presumably for viewing actual specimens not visible in photo). No catalog numbers visible.

text.en: From pollination to decomposition, flies perform important roles in nearly every ecosystem. Crane flies (Tipulidae) usually don't eat anything as adults, but their larvae often help break down decaying plants. Robber flies (Asilidae) stab and drain insect prey with their beak-like mouthparts. Bee flies (Bombyliidae) look like bumblebees and often pollinate plants.

text.en: "If all mankind were to disappear, the world would regenerate back to the rich state of equilibrium that existed ten thousand years ago. If insects were to vanish, the environment would collapse into chaos." — Edward O. Wilson

text.en: In the Burgess Shale, in Canada's Rockies, thousands of marine animals were fossilized 505 million years ago. The unusual, detailed preservation of these animals' soft parts offers a rare window into our deepest evolutionary past, displaying ancient ancestors of modern groups alongside unique, extinct lineages. Marella is unique, but shares a common ancestor with arthropods such as trilobites, crustaceans, and horseshoe crabs. This scaly animal could be an ancestor of segmented worms or molluscs — or could belong to an extinct group.

text.en: Anomalocaris hunted the oceans that covered British Columbia 500 million years ago. It took scientists nearly a century to discover what the animal really looked like, because most fossils showed only parts of its body. Which part of Anomalocaris do you think these fossils show?

text.en: The chambered nautilus is one of only a few modern descendants of ancient nautiloids. The nautiloids evolved quickly in the Ordovician to become the ocean's top predator, gobbling up early fish and other sea creatures. Some had coiled shells, others straight. The biggest were a massive 10 metres in length — the largest animal that, until then, had ever lived.

text.en: Large coral reefs became more common in the Silurian, a time when marine life flourished and diversified in warm and shallow seas. This wasn't entirely coincidence. Scientists now know that coral reefs are hot spots for new species to evolve.

text.en: Placoderms were well-protected with armour and spines. Known as "the age of fish," the Devonian had an amazing diversity of fish — both weird and wonderful — that are now extinct. Eusthenopteron was once considered the "missing link" between fish and tetrapods.

text.en: Long-extinct sea creatures left these fossils, but the animals looked and acted like their modern relatives. Like sea anemones and modern corals, these corals fed with tentacles around their mouths. Devonian brittle stars look similar to modern ones and move the same way — using their flexible arms. Solitary rugose corals are often called horn corals. Today there are about 1,500 species of modern brittle stars.

text.en: Mesosaurus was one of the first reptiles to go back to living in the water where its amphibian ancestors had once lived. Like the modern crocodile, it had nostrils at the top of its jaws and needed to keep its head at the water's surface to breathe. Mesosaurus, which became extinct about 270 million years ago, has been found in Africa and eastern South America—evidence that these two continents were once joined.

details.notes: Large red illustration of Mesosaurus at top. Map showing Africa, South America, India, Antarctica, Australia with Mesosaurus locations marked. Fossil specimen displayed at lower left.

text.en: These leaflets are a fossil of Walchia, an evergreen tree that thrived about 300 million years ago. This tiny animal, Branchiosaurus (not to be mistaken with Brachiosaurus, the biggest dinosaur that ever roamed Earth!), is an early amphibian that lived at the same time as Walchia.

text.en: Monotis, or paper clams, lived about 200 million years ago. Their fossils have been found in British Columbia, but also as far away as Austria, the Himalayas, and Nevada. We don't know why they were so widespread, but some hypothesize they might have travelled by attaching themselves to floating masses of seaweed.

text.en: Fossils from heaven and hell? These fascinating fossils have puzzled and enchanted people for thousands of years. Fossil echinoids are sometimes known as "fairy loaves" because of their resemblance to a round loaf. Keep one in your home and you will always have bread. English folklore tells of "thunderbolts" (belemnites) thrown down from the heavens during storms and "devil's toenails" (Gryphaea) cast off the devil himself.

details.notes: Multiple fossil types displayed illustrating folklore associations. Three echinoids at center, belemnite specimens at left (single and tray of five), Gryphaea specimens at lower right with blue tape.

text.en: Even though insects are everywhere, and we think of them as hardy, it's rare for them to be fossilized, since their outer skeleton, known as an exoskeleton, is actually quite delicate. The oldest known fossilized insect is about 400 million years old, making insects among the first animals to live on land.

text.en: Phareodus testis is an extinct fish species that lived approximately 50 million years ago. This fossil is from the Green River Formation in Wyoming where periodic blooms of blue-green algae caused low oxygen levels in the river, suffocating the fish. As they sank to the bottom they were gradually covered in fine-grained limestone mud. Repeated episodes over millions of years created layers of some of the world's best-preserved fossils. Phareodus testis has some distant living relatives today, including the goldeye found in northern Canada, and several types of freshwater arowana fish.

details.notes: Large complete fish fossil displayed. Red fish outline illustrations in background. Map of North America with Green River Formation location marked. Handwritten label on specimen reads partially: 'Approved for personal display' and additional text.

text.en: "Rosa ×engelmannii subsp. britannicae-columbiae is named for the province of British Columbia, where my early Rosa education at the University of British Columbia led to my lifetime study of Rosa in North America." -Dr Walter H. Lewis, pictured with Dr. Margery Eliot-Lewis in the Beaty Biodiversity Museum in 2016. The British Columbia rose was found within our collections and named as a new hybrid in 2016 by rose expert and UBC alumnus, Dr. Walter H. Lewis. This specimen was collected in 1953 and first identified as our common Rosa woodsii with the collector knowing the name didn't quite fit the plant's morphology. Now, DNA technology has revealed this species' complex parental combination as a hybrid new to science.

text.en: THE DIANA G. HORTON AND DAVID W. JAMIESON COLLECTIONS. Many of Dr. Hortons specimens are Encalypta, the genus of moss her research focused on. These include several type specimens described by Dr. Horton. Types are natural history specimens scientists use to describe species new to science. From the South Shetlands to Svalbard, thousands of the specimens in the Beaty Biodiversity Museum's bryophyte collection come from bryologists Dr. Diana G. Horton and Dr. David W. Jamieson, generously donated by Dr. Hortons sister, Patricia Webb. This world-class collection contains bryophytes collected from over 80 countries and territories across all seven continents, from both Dr. Hortons extensive collecting and exchange of specimens with researchers and institutions around the world.

text.en: Starting in 2004, mycologist Oluna Ceska conducted an almost-15-year survey of the fungi of Observatory Hill in Saanich, British Columbia. During her 40-50 visits each year, Oluna found around 1,450 species of fungi, many of which she collected and are now housed here at the Beaty Biodiversity Museum. Scientists estimate that there are one million species of fungi around the world which remain unknown to science; 10,000 of which are located in BC. The work of collectors such as Oluna Ceska is incredibly valuable to scientists working to identify these unknown species. In recognition of Oluna's extensive collections and contributions to Canadian mycology, two species she discovered at Observatory Hill were named after her: Inocybe ceskae and Cortinarius ceskarumfceskae.

details.notes: Shadowbox about mycologist Oluna Ceska and her fungi survey of Observatory Hill, Saanich, BC. text.en: Natural history collections can predict the effects of global climate change. Researchers can use pressed plant specimens to compare the flowering date with annual temperature records. Scientists were able to determine plants at higher elevations and those which bloom earlier in the season are more sensitive to warming temperatures. Thimbleberry blooms 4.4 days earlier for every degree of warming. Barbara Neto-Bradley, one of the scientists behind this research, completed her MSc in Botany in the Whitton and Pennell labs at UBC's Biodiversity Research Centre. Listen to Barbara talk about some more work on leaf shape and plant evolution here: https://explore.beatymuseum.ubc.ca/researchers-revealed/b_neto-bradley/q/ Linda P.J. Lipsen, another scientist on this study, is the Vascular Plant and Algae Collections Curator at the Beaty Biodiversity Museum. You can learn more about pressed plants and their importance in research here: https://explore.beatymuseum.ubc.ca/pressed-plants/q/ Kopp, C.W., Neto-Bradley, B., Lipsen, L.P.J., Jas, S., & Smith, S. (2020). Herbarium records indicate variation in bloom-time sensitivity to temperature across a geographically diverse region. International Journal of Biometeorology, 64(5), 873-880. doi: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00484-020-01877-1

text.en: Huber Moore was a true community scientist and a unique collector of nature. Originally from Milton, Ontario, his father was a farmer and taught Huber the local birds and plants, sparking Huber's interest in the natural world. He had a keen interest in birds, butterflies, vascular plants, and mosses and had a unique way of documenting and storing his collections. His collection exhibits the importance of community collectors for science and art. With no formal education in sciences, his work shows that higher education is not necessary to be involved and make an impact in the scientific community and conservation efforts. Our goal is to showcase his unique collection and make it accessible for scientists, artists, and all those who may be inspired by his life's work. Learn more about the Huber Moore collection here. To leave feedback, email info@beatymuseum.ubc.ca

The youngest species on the planet?
It could be British Columbia's three-
spine sticklebacks. As glaciers
retreated after the last ice age, marine
sticklebacks colonized BC lakes,
but with unique results. Freshwater
sticklebacks are found throughout

Darwin was right, and sticklebacks
prove it. Threespine sticklebacks in
isolated BC lakes have repeatedly
evolved the same "species pairs" -a
smaller, open-water (limnetic) fish and
a larger, bottom-dwelling (benthic)
fish. Limnetics and benthics from
the same lake do not interbreed, but
when researchers placed benthics from
different lakes together, they were able
to interbreed. This supports Darwin's
theory of natural selection, which
contends that populations of a species
will evolve in similar ways given the
same environmental conditions.

four species living in tropical waters.
They can reach two metres in length
and have a narrow, tubular body, a

vertically, as if they are floating twigs.
When unsuspecting prey come near, the
cornetfish darts forward and rapidly
expands its mouth to suck in a victim.

These specimens have been
cleared and stained. First a
chemical bath turns specimens semi-
transparent, then stains are used to
highlight specific tissues, particularly
cartilage (blue) and bone (red).
Scientists often count ribs and fin
rays in order to identify fish, but fish
bones can be tiny and difficult to
see. Clearing and staining specimens
can highlight important structures
without the messy work of dissection.

A glacial relict? Deepwater sculpins
are found in the deep, cold freshwater
of Canada's largest lakes. Strangely,
their closest relative lives in the Arctic
Ocean. According to the "glacial
sluicing" hypothesis, as glaciers
advanced, they scooped up marine
populations from the Artic and carried
them southwards. When the ice sheets
retreated, these populations were
stranded in the large bodies of melted
glacier water that we know as lakes.

image_transcriptions.text:
Finding a mate can be hard. But some fish have evolved a way
to beat the odds - they change sex. Some hermaphroditic fish
change sex once in their lives, some switch back and forth, and
some can be both sexes at the same time.
1. Zebra goby
Lythrypnus zebra
Braithwaite Bay, Mexico, 1957
No. BC57-0160
2. Blackeye goby
Coryphopterus nicholsi
Howe Sound, BC, 1963
No. BC63-1007
3. Orange clownfish
Amphiprion percula
Vancouver Aquarium,
BC, 1959
No. BCS9-0307
The zebra goby is a
simultaneous hermaphrodite,
meaning that it has both
male and female reproductive
organs at the same time.
Born female, blackeye gobies
start reproducing when they are
6 to 10 centimetres long. When
they reach 10 to 20 centimetres,
they change into males. These
are sequential hermaphrodites.
Groups of male clownfish live
under the control of a larger
female. When the female dies,
the dominant male changes sex
to become the leader queen.
4. Marbled parrotfish
Leptoscarus vaigiensis
Easter Island, Chile, 1965
No. BC6S-0431
The marbled parrotfish is the
only one of more than 80
species of parrotfish that does
not change from female to
male during its life.

delivering live births, and fertilizing
eggs internally or externally. Most
fish reproduce through external
fertilisation. Typically, females lay
thousands of eggs while males release
sperm, and hopefully eggs and sperm
meet. With internal fertilisation, eggs
are either incubated internally but
receive no maternal nourishment, or
the mother directly nourishes her
young with a mammal-like placenta
and gives birth to fully-formed fry.

When fish stay together, they are
"shoaling." When they swim together, we say
they are "schooling." There are many benefits
of shoaling and schooling-safety in numbers,
energy efficiency, and enormous numbers of
potential mates. The most spectacular schools
often occur during migrations, when many
populations aggregate together.
1. South American pilchard
Sardinops sagax
San Diego, California, 1929
No. BC61-0619
Millions of South American pilchard
migrate each year from South Africa to
Mozambique, causing a feeding frenzy
among predators along the coast.
2. Pacific herring
Clupea pallasii pallasii
Baynes Sound, BC, 1954
No. BCSS-0054
Pacific herring spawn in vast schools,
producing up to six million eggs per
square metre.

Stegastes fasciolatus
Easter Island, Chile, 1965
No. BC65-0438
The Pacific gregory is so territorial that
other species of fish sometimes feed in
schools, rather than individually,for
protection from its assaults.

Rangiroa Reef, French Polynesia, 1961

Like many reef fish, butterflyfishes shoal
together for safety.

example of adaptation. Their modified
dorsal fin forms an oval sucker,
with which they attach themselves

relationship. Remoras, however,
receive transportation, protection,
and scraps from their hosts' meals.

Coral reefs are created by colonies
of tiny polyps, which build hard
skeletons throughout their lives. As
generations of these minuscule animals
live and die, they slowly build the
ocean's most complex habitat. Not
surprisingly, many fish have evolved
specializations for reef life. Many
are flattened side-to-side for quick
motions and manoeuvrability. Some
have beak-like mouths for scraping
algae off coral. Most are vibrantly
coloured and patterned, though
preserved fish lose most of their colour.

It's hard for fish to keep clean
without hands, but señoritas and
other cleaner fish can help. They feed
on parasites and dead skin from fish
that congregate at cleaning stations.
A fish in need of cleaning swims into
a station, opens its mouth, and hovers.
Not all fish are as helpful as cleaner
fish. The sabre-tooth blenny looks just
like a cleaner fish, but when an
unsuspecting fish offers itself for
cleaning, the blenny bites a chunk of
flesh and rushes away.

text.en:
It's hard for fish to keep clean
without hands, but señoritas and
other cleaner fish can help. They feed
on parasites and dead skin from fish
that congregate at cleaning stations.
A fish in need of cleaning swims into
a station, opens its mouth, and hovers.
Not all fish are as helpful as cleaner
fish. The sabre-tooth blenny looks just
like a cleaner fish, but when an
unsuspecting fish offers itself for
cleaning, the blenny bites a chunk of
flesh and rushes away.

Squirrelfishes and soldierfishes are
part of the family Holocentridae. Big-
eyed and nocturnal, these reef fish are
mostly red, a seemingly highly visible
colour that actually camouflages the fish.
Red light is filtered out in deep and dark
waters, making red fish difficult to see.
When threatened, squirrelfishes make
warning grunts with their swim bladders.
Many also have venomous spines.

The migrating eye of flatfishes is
a tascinating story of evolutionary
change. As flatfishes adapted to
swimming on their side along the
ocean floor, their lower eye was
rendered all but useless. As a result, a
remarkable adaptation occurred - the
lower eye migrated over to the top
side. Even more bizarre, flatfishes
are born with one eye on either side
of their heads. The eye migration
occurs during the fish's young life.

Fish have a sixth sense. In addition
to our five senses, most fish have
a "lateral line" running along both

and generate electrical impulses.

How do fish see in the dark?
Nocturnal fish often have oversized
eyes or sensitive, whisker-like barbels
for sensing objects in dark waters.
Most spectacularly, many deep-sea
fish have evolved an ability to use
chemicals within their bodies or light-
generating bacteria to produce light,
known as bioluminescense. Some
fish flash their lights as a warning,
to attract mates, or even as a lure.

Deep-sea lanternfishes are named for
their photophores, or light-producing
organs. Each of the 246 species has a
different arrangement of photophores,
which suggests that the fish use
bioluminescence to communicate. With
a global biomass of over 550 million
tonnes, lanternfishes are among the
most widely distributed and abundant
of all vertebrates, and they play a vital
link in the food chain, connecting
zooplankton to larger marine animals.

American eels link freshwater and
marine ecosystems, transporting
nutrients from one part of the world
to another. The eels hatch in the
Sargasso Sea and drift westwards for
nearly a year. When they reach the
North American coast, they migrate
up estuaries and streams. After
living in freshwater for between five
and twenty years, the eels become
sexually mature, and begin their
8000 kilometre migration back to the
Sargasso Sea to reproduce and die.
American eel
Anguilla rostrata

Our lungs and a fish's swim bladder
are evolutionarily related. Both
evolved from early fish lungs, which
helped fish survive in low oxygen
conditions millions of years ago. In
many fish, these lungs developed
into a swim bladder, a gas-filled sack
that sits just above a fish's gut. By
controlling air pressure in their swim
bladder, fish maintain stability and
buoyancy at different depths or while
remaining still.
1. Pacific nurse shark (likely)

The Cyprinidae are the largest family
of freshwater fish. In fact, with over
2,600 species, they may be the largest
family of vertebrates. Faced with
such enormous diversity, scientists
have struggled to resolve the
family's phylogeny, that is, how the
species are evolutionarily related to
each other and to other families. At
least 13 subfamilies have been
proposed, but the exact number is
still under debate.

Water is about 800 times denser
than air, which presents a special
challenge to underwater predators.
As they lunge toward prey, their
movement forces water forward
and pushes the prey farther away.
Predatory fish have evolved specialized
techniques for getting food in spite of
the water between predator and prey.
1. Pacific herring
Clupea pallasii pallasii
Unga Strait, Alaska, 1964
No. BC65-0084

swim open-mouthed,
filtering prey from
the water as it passes
through their gills.
2. Moray eel

Rangiroa, French
Polynesia, 1961
No. BC62-0253
Like many fish, moray eels
use surprise tactics. They
hide in cracks and crevices
until their prey is within
reach, then lunge out.
3. Red cornetfish
Fistularia petimba
Cape San Lucas, Mexico, 1957
No. BC57-0140
By rapidly expanding
their snouts, cornetfish
create negative pressure
in and around their jaws,
which vacuums prey in.

into the air.

Pikes are built for ambush. Their
mottled skin camouflages them as
they sit and wait. Their dorsal and
anal fins are set very close to their
tail fin. This anatomy helps
generate sudden bursts of speed,
helping pikes thrust out of hiding
toward prey. Plus, their large jaws
and sharp, pointed teeth make sure
the surprised fish does not escape.

mottled skin camouflages them as

anal fins are set very close to their

generate sudden bursts of speed,
helping pikes thrust out of hiding
toward prey. Plus, their large jaws
and sharp, pointed teeth make sure
the surprised fish does not escape.

Preserving biodiversity is important,
even at the population level.
Sockeye salmon from Bristol Bay,
Alaska, support one of the world's
most valuable and dependable
fisheries, largely because the
species has diversified into
hundreds of local populations,
each with a different life cycle,
each adapted to its own river.
Because each population is suited
to different conditions, the species
as a whole and the fishery thrive
each year even if some
populations are low.

Pacific salmon: British Columbia's
provincial fishes.
There are five species of Pacific salmon native
to British Columbia: the Chinook, sockeye,
chum, pink, and coho salmon. There are
also two species of Pacific trout native to
BC: the rainbow and cutthroat trouts.
In 2013, Pacific salmon collectively were
officially adopted as BC's "provincial fish"
owing to their tremendous biological,
historical, cultural, and economic
significance to BC. With this designation,
they join other iconic animals and plants,
such as the Steller's jay, the Kermode "Spirit
Bear', western redcedar, and the Pacific
dogwood as emblems of BC biodiversity.

salmon will hatch the next year.

image_transcriptions.text:
Spawning salmon are crucial to the
balance of British Columbia's coastal
ecosystems. Salmon fatten in the
ocean before swimming inland to
spawn and die. These returning
salmon bring a huge source of new
nutrients into the area. Predators and
scavengers gorge on the spawners,
often dragging carcasses into
surrounding forests. Forests are
fertilized by salmon remains and
animal droppings. In turn, forests
provide shade, shelter, and
sustenance for an abundance of life.

The order Stomiiformes contains some
rather bizarre-looking deep-sea fish,
including viperfishes, snaggletooths,
bristlemouths, and loosejaws. As their
common names suggest, most of these
fish have exaggerated fangs and
oversized mouths. Like many
deep-sea fish, Stomiiformes produce
bioluminescence, usually as rows of
glowing spots along their bodies.
Some species also have a luminescent
barbel dangling from their lower jaw
to lure prey.

whitefishes. All salmonids spawn
in freshwater, although many species
spend much of their lives at sea.
These seagoing species live one
to five years in the ocean before
embarking on their amazing
journey "home" to freshwater.
Some travel hundreds of kilometres
and climb hundreds of metres to reach
their natal streams, where they
reproduce and usually die afterwards.

a sleek body for rapid swimming, every

Fish are the oldest and most diverse
group of vertebrates, and these two
characteristics are connected. In
some groups, the entire fish genome
has doubled three times, once more
than any other vertebrate group.
Such duplication events usually
generate diversity. With two of
every gene, one gene can maintain
the original function while the
other can mutate into a new form,
which means genetic "experiments"
can occur without harming the
organism's overall well-being.

The amazing diversity of fish has
arisen in part from their remarkable
ability for ecological specialization.

to the darkest depths of the ocean,
from tropical swamps to tide pools,

extreme and diverse habitats than any
other vertebrate group.

Lampreys and hagfishes have no true
jaws. Lampreys feed on body fluids
by attaching their mouth to a living
animal and injecting its flesh with an
anti-clotting fluid. Hagfishes mainly
eat dead and dying sea creatures,
often entering their victim's bodies to
devour them from the inside. When
threatened, hagfish can also create a
defensive slime formed from special
fibres mixed with the surrounding
seawater.

image_transcriptions.text:
Sharks are in the class Chondrichthyes,
or cartilaginous fishes, meaning their
skeletons are made of cartilage rather
than bone. Although Condricthyes are
among the oldest living vertebrates, intact
shark fossils are rare because cartilage
decomposes more rapidly than bones
or teeth. Luckily, sharks replace teeth
at an extraordinary rate - up to several
thousand in a lifetime, which means early
shark-tooth fossils are abundant.

Among the most archaic of fish.
sturgeons are known for their
clongated bodies lined with sharp.
bony projections, cartilagenous
skeletons, often enormous length
(up to five metres), and roe, or
caviar. Sturgeons may also be the
longest-lived fish. Some species live
over a century and only reach sexual
maturity at age 20. Because of their
slow reproductive rate, the desirability
of their roe, and their susceptibility to
habitat degradation, almost all species
are under threat.

Acipenser transmontanus

sponge reefs were discovered off the BC
coast. They're thought to be 9,000 years
old and to exist nowhere else on Earth.

Half of all bird species belong to one
order: Passeriformes. Often called
"perching birds" or "song birds,"
passerines have "perching" feet with
three toes pointing forward and one toe
backwards. Their leg muscles evolved to
tighten while perching, allowing the birds
to sleep without falling off branches. One
explanation for the amazing diversity
of passerines is their sophisticated vocal
abilities, which enables diverse tones and
dialects. Distinctive songs may encourage
discrete communities, and possibly lead to
new species.

The eggs of common murres are
beautifully distinctive. Murres
gather in enormous, densely packed
colonies perched on cliffs to lay eggs
and raise chicks. Frequently, ten to
twenty couples lay eggs within a
square metre. Luckily, each egg has
a unique colour and pattern to help
parents keep track of their egg. Also,
its pear shape helps the egg roll in
a circle rather than off the cliff.

eagles, hawks, vultures, and owls have more
light receptors in their retinas than humans,
giving them spectacular long-distance vision
and allowing them to see at least four times
more detail. They also have large forward-
facing eyes for binocular vision. Owls and
other nocturnal hunters ofthen lack cone cells
(colour receptors), since colour vision is less
important at night.

The Wilson Journal of Ornithology 129(2):411-416, 2017
First Record of House Swift (Apus nipalensis) in the Americas
Ildiko Szabo,!3^ Kimberly Walters,? James Rourke," and Darren E. Irwin'
ABSTRACT.—A carcass of a House Swift (Apus
nipalensis) found in Ladner, British Columbia on 18 May
2012 appears to be the first documented rocord of this
species in the Americas. Identification is based on DNA
sequencing and morphometric charaeters. University of
British Columbia Beaty Biodiversity Museum Cowan
Tetrapod Collection catalogue number B017056 has been
assigned to this specimen (round study skin, sproad wing.
partial skeleton, and tissue samples). Received 10 June 2016.
Accepted 21 November 2016.
In the course of a bird survey conducted by
Hemmera Envirochem Inc. (Hemmera; Bumaby,
British Columbia, Canada) on 18May 2012 along
the Deltaport container terminal causeway in Ladner,
British Columbia, an unidentified swift was found
and photographed (Fig. I) by Kimberly Walters and
Brock Ramshaw. This site is -40 m from the Pacific
Ocean (49° 2' 48.959" N, 123° 7' 40.088" W). The
swift carcass was frozen in sample bag KW-120518-
02-456-03 as per Hemmera's field sampling proto-
cols and stored for later identification. Because the
swift did not appear to be a known North American
species, the specimen was transferred to the
University of British Columbia Beaty Biodiversity
(UBCBBM) Cowan Tetrapod Collection (CTC) on 9
September 2013 (by J.R. and K.W.) for the purpose
of identifying the species of the swift and preserving
the specimen.
Cowan Tetrapod Collection. Beaty Biodiversity Museum.
University of British Columbia, 2212 Main Mall, Vancouver.
BC. V6T 1Z4. Canada
Environmental Assessment Office, 836 Yates Street, PO Box
9426 Stn Prov Govt, Victoria, BC, VSW 9V1. Canada
Hemmera, 18-4730 Kingsway, Bumnaby, BC, VSH 0C6.Canada
Corresponding author: email: ildiko@zoology.ubc.ca/
FIG. 1. Unidentified swifl just before it was salvaged.
METHODS
On 14 October 2014, the swift was prepared as
UBCBBM-CTC specimen No. B017056 (round
study skin, spread wing (left], partial skeleton, and
three frozen tissue samples). UBCBBM-CTC
tissue catalog number TB000756 is fresh liver.
heart, and breast muscle. Two minced tissue
samples (both labeled ISZ0370) were preserved.
one in DMSO bufler and one in 95% cthanol.
Morphological measurements and general body
condition were assessed.
Muscle sample (in 95% ethanol) was sent to the
Canadian Centre for DNA Barcoding (CCDB) for
sequencing of the cytochrome oxidase subunit 1
(COl) gene. The CCDB received the sample on 5
February 2014 and issued a final report on 26
March 26 2014. Bidirectional forward and reverse
sequences were generated using PCR with univer-
sal primer cocktails for birds and mammals,
BirdF1 tl + COlbirdR2 tl and C VFILFU +
C_VRILRt1, using a BigDye Terminator v3.1 kit
and an ABI 3730xL DNA Analyzer (Applied
Biosystems Inc., Foster City, CA, USA).
This COl gene sequence has been deposited to
Genbank with accession number KY242302.
Additional tissue, a study skin, and partial skeleton
havealreadybeen deposited as B017056 in the
University of British Columbia Beaty Biodiversity
Museum avian collection.

This house swift is the first documented record of
the species in the Americas. The bird was found
in Ladner, British Columbia in 2012 and brought
to the Beaty Biodiversity Museum. Its identity
was confirmed using a combination of methods
including analysis of DNA, plumage colouration,
and body measurements.
House swifts usually range from Nepal to Japan and
are not known to migrate long distances. Why this
male house swift flew to BC remains a mystery.

ABSTRACT.—A carcass of a House Swift (Apus
nipalensis) found in Ladner, British Columbia on 18 May
2012 appears to be the first documented rocord of this
species in the Americas. Identification is based on DNA
sequencing and morphometric charaeters. University of
British Columbia Beaty Biodiversity Museum Cowan
Tetrapod Collection catalogue number B017056 has been
assigned to this specimen (round study skin, sproad wing.
partial skeleton, and tissue samples). Received 10 June 2016.
Accepted 21 November 2016.
In the course of a bird survey conducted by
Hemmera Envirochem Inc. (Hemmera; Bumaby,
British Columbia, Canada) on 18May 2012 along
the Deltaport container terminal causeway in Ladner,
British Columbia, an unidentified swift was found
and photographed (Fig. I) by Kimberly Walters and
Brock Ramshaw. This site is -40 m from the Pacific
Ocean (49° 2' 48.959" N, 123° 7' 40.088" W). The
swift carcass was frozen in sample bag KW-120518-
02-456-03 as per Hemmera's field sampling proto-
cols and stored for later identification. Because the
swift did not appear to be a known North American
species, the specimen was transferred to the
University of British Columbia Beaty Biodiversity
(UBCBBM) Cowan Tetrapod Collection (CTC) on 9
September 2013 (by J.R. and K.W.) for the purpose
of identifying the species of the swift and preserving
the specimen.

Dr. Jessica Ulrika Meir
is a physiologist and astronaut who
launched to space in a Soyuz capsule
in 2019. Meir spent 205 days aboard
the International Space Station, where
she conducted hundreds of scientific
experiments. Jessica went on three
spacewalks, including the first all-
female spacewalk in human history.
When she was a postdoctoral fellow
at UBC, she conducted windtunnel
experiments on bar-headed goose
physiology during high-altitude flight
conditions.
"I took these feathers to space
with me to represent a pivotal
chapter of my life (both
professionally and personally)
as a post-doc at UBC, and as
an aid to facilitate scientific
education and outreach. I also
felt that it was symbolic to
bring a piece of this iconic high-
altitude species, the bar-headed
goose, to an even greater height."

is later broken up in the gizzard. Beaks
wear down with use and grow continually

Galliformes are an order of round-bodied,
ground-dwelling birds that include such
familiar species as chickens and turkeys.
Often called "game birds," Galliformes also

partridge, and pheasant, that are hunted

Hedgehogs, porcupines, and echidnas
all have spines forprotection, but that
doesn't mean they share a spiny
ancestor. Echidnas are monotremes,
porcupines are rodents, and hedgehogs
are erinaceids. Each evolved spines
independently as a result of convergent
evolution, a process by which unrelated
creatures evolve similar features.
Convergent evolution is responsible for
many striking similarities between only
distantly related animals and can often
make classification difficult.

Evolution works through a series
of slight mutations to existing
characteristics. Over thousands
or millions of generations, such
incremental changes can completely
alter how animals look and live.
Adaptation is usually driven by
competition and survival. Some
features are more useful than
others, allowing certain animals
to thrive while others struggle
with less advantageous traits.
1. Sunda pangolin
Manis javanica
Simanggang, Malaysia, 1961
No. 8722
The pangolin's tongue is not
attached in its throat, but
to a bone near its pelvis.
3. North island brown kiwi
Apteryx australis
New Zealand
No. 9599
The kiwi's nostrils are
located at the end of
its long beak, to locate
insects and worms
underground by smell.
2. White-throated toucan
Ramphastos toucanus
No. 15798
The toucan's bill is a

within a few minutes.

highly sensitive
touch receptors.

image_transcriptions.text:
Marsupials and monotremes
include some very unusual mammals.
Monotremes - platypuses and
echidnas -are the only mammals to lay
eggs. Lacking nipples, they excrete milk
through pores in their skin. Marsupials,
or "pouched" mammals, give birth
to nearly embryonic newborns. Once
the tiny joey, as it is called, crawls into
the mother's pouch, it latches onto a
nipple until it is fully developed. The
nearly 300 species of marsupials include
kangaroos, wombats, opossums,
koalas, and Tasmanian devils.

footed." Tetrapods are animals that
have four legs or whose ancestors
had four legs. This means that snakes,
birds, and humans are tetrapods.

image_transcriptions.text:
Rampant poaching in the 1970s
reduced the black rhino population
in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania,
from over 800 to fewer than 20
animals. The Serengeti Biodiversity
Program at UBC is part of a
mega-relocation project working to
relocate 32 black rhinos from South
Africa into the Serengeti National
Park. In 2010 the first six rhinos were
successfully relocated.
Black rhinoceros
Diceros bicornis

image_transcriptions.text:
Mouse-deer escape predators by diving
into water and swimming underwater to
safety. Although unusual for deer, this
watery getaway may hint at evolutionary
history. In 2007, a fossil was discovered in
India of an extinct, small deer-like animal,
Indohyus, with bones adapted for life in the
water. Its aquatic adaptations suggest that
Indohyus could be an early ancestor of whales
and may be a "missing link" between whales
and land mammals.
Mouse-deer
Tragulus sp.
No. 8918

Cranial sutures are the jagged joints
that connect the different bones of the
skull. The skull is composed of multiple
bony plates for several reasons. They
allow the skull to expand easily as an
animal grows, and the sutures give the
skull slight elasticity in case of trauma.
Animals with heavy antlers often have
complex suture joints for extra strength.

When tracking population
movements, sometimes the least
direct route is the most likely. DNA
analysis reveals that white-tailed
deer spread down the east coast of
North America, across Mexico, and
up the west coast, where populations
evolved into black-tailed deer. Black-
tails spread castward and bred with
westward-drifting white-tails. These
hybrids eventually became mule deer.
However, it was long believed that
white-tails simply spread westward,
and that black-tails-not mule deer-
were the youngest American deer.

ARTIST STATEMENT
De Daphne Boyer,
artiste en arts visuels et phytologue:
« Les cuvres que vous voyez dans Li bootee
mishiwayitay
- The Beauty of It All ont été
réalisées à partir de techniques artisanales
traditionnelles pratiquées surtout par des
remmes, d'outils numériques, de matériaux
végétaux et de piquants de porc-épic.
Cette exposition rend hommage à trois femmes
: mon arrière-grand-mère Éléonore, née lors
d'une chasse au bison et qui fut sage-femme
itinérante; ma grand-mère Clémence, une
interprète michif-français-anglais qui cacha ses
origines autochtones pour protéger ses quinze
erifants : ma mère Anita, naturaliste, conteuse et
archiviste familtale, qui a inspiré ma génération
à célébrer notre héritage Métis.
Pour nombre d'ocuvres, J'ai utilisé des
techniques numériques de perlage et de travall
des piquants de porc-épic, techniques que
Jai mises au point en m'inspirant du travail
méticuleux de mes ancêtres lorsqu'elles
décoraient des vêtements ou des outils. Toutes
mes créations sont originales et n'ont pas été
téléchargées d'internet.
De nouvelles ocuvres explorent les écosystèmes
des Prairies qui ont abrité et nourri les Premlères
Nations, les Métis et tout ce qui y vit depuis
des temps immémoriaux, et notamment "L1
tayrayn araa en rivyayr - The Watershed", une
ceinture fléchée Métis longue de huit mètres
tissée au doigt, créée en collaboration avec Matt
Hiitermann, un historien et artisan, et inspirée des
vastes bassins migratoires des Grandes plaines. »
Je tiens à remercler Don Sugden pour son travail de
rédaction et de révision, ainsi qu'Emmanuel Hérique
pour les traductions en français.
My name is Daphne Boyer.
1am a visual artist and plant scientist.
The works you see in Li bootee mishiwayitay
- The Beauty of It All were created using
women's traditional handwork, digital tools,
plant materlals, and porcupine quills.
This exhibition honours my great-
grandmother Eléonore, an itinerant midwife
who was born on a buffalo hunt; my
grandmother Clémence, a Michif-French-
English interpreter who hid her Indigenous
ancestry to protect her 15 children; and my
mother Anita, a naturalist, storyteller, and
tamily archivist who inspired my generation
to celebrate our Métis ancestry.
Many works were created using digital
beading and digital quillwork techniques
1 developed which echo the meticulous
handwork employed by my ancestors to
adorn clothing and tools. All my designs are
original (not downloaded from the Internet).
Now pleces explore Prairie ecosystems that
have sustalned First Nations/ Métis, and all
living beings since time immemorial, including
"Li tayrayn araa en rivyayr - The Watershed"
an eight-metre finger-woven Métis sash
co-created with historian and artisan
Matt Hiltermann, and inspired by the vast
migratory watersheds of the Great Plains.
I would like to thank Don Sugden for his
writing and editing work as well as Emmanuel
Hérique for the French translations

: mon arrière-grand-mère Éléonore, née lors
d'une chasse au bison et qui fut sage-femme
itinérante; ma grand-mère Clémence, une
interprète michif-français-anglais qui cacha ses
origines autochtones pour protéger ses quinze
erifants : ma mère Anita, naturaliste, conteuse et
archiviste familtale, qui a inspiré ma génération
à célébrer notre héritage Métis.
Pour nombre d'ocuvres, J'ai utilisé des
techniques numériques de perlage et de travall
des piquants de porc-épic, techniques que
Jai mises au point en m'inspirant du travail
méticuleux de mes ancêtres lorsqu'elles
décoraient des vêtements ou des outils. Toutes
mes créations sont originales et n'ont pas été
téléchargées d'internet.
De nouvelles ocuvres explorent les écosystèmes
des Prairies qui ont abrité et nourri les Premlères
Nations, les Métis et tout ce qui y vit depuis
des temps immémoriaux, et notamment "L1
tayrayn araa en rivyayr - The Watershed", une
ceinture fléchée Métis longue de huit mètres
tissée au doigt, créée en collaboration avec Matt
Hiitermann, un historien et artisan, et inspirée des
vastes bassins migratoires des Grandes plaines. »
Je tiens à remercler Don Sugden pour son travail de
rédaction et de révision, ainsi qu'Emmanuel Hérique
pour les traductions en français.
My name is Daphne Boyer.
1am a visual artist and plant scientist.
The works you see in Li bootee mishiwayitay
- The Beauty of It All were created using
women's traditional handwork, digital tools,
plant materlals, and porcupine quills.
This exhibition honours my great-
grandmother Eléonore, an itinerant midwife
who was born on a buffalo hunt; my
grandmother Clémence, a Michif-French-
English interpreter who hid her Indigenous
ancestry to protect her 15 children; and my
mother Anita, a naturalist, storyteller, and
tamily archivist who inspired my generation
to celebrate our Métis ancestry.
Many works were created using digital
beading and digital quillwork techniques
1 developed which echo the meticulous
handwork employed by my ancestors to
adorn clothing and tools. All my designs are

an eight-metre finger-woven Métis sash
co-created with historian and artisan

migratory watersheds of the Great Plains.

writing and editing work as well as Emmanuel

image_transcriptions.text:
BIO
Daphne Boyer est une artiste en arts visuels et
phytologue canadienne qui combine matériaux
végétaux, piquants de porc-épic, outils numériques
haute résolution et techniques artisanales
traditionnelles pour créer des œuvres d'art qui
rendent hommage à son héritage Métis de la rivière
Rouge et font entrer les plantes et les animaux
comme des membres de sa propre famille.
Sa passion pour le monde naturel a commencé
dans les prairies de la Saskatchewan, lors
des randonnées qu'elle faisait avec sa mère
naturaliste. Cette expérience de jeunesse a
évelllé un intérêt pour la guérison par les
herbes et pour l'étude de la botanique, intérét
qui perdure à ce jour. En 2017, à l'age de 62 ans,
elle crée un atelier et inventera un langage
visuel mettant en scène les plantes qui sont
Importantes dans la culture Métis.
Le travail de Daphne Boyer se fait l'écho des
récits intergénérationnels sur la famille, le
terroir et le savoir Métis. Les cuvres qu'elle
propose sont réalisées grice à deux techniques
qu'elle a mises au point : le perlage numérique
et le travall numérique des piquants de porc-
éplc. Les motifs récurrents reflètent les récits
intergénérationnels qu'elle raconte.
Son travail bénéficie du soutien du Conseil des arts
du Canada, du First Peoples Cultural Council et du
Conseil des arts et des lettres du Québec.
Daphne Boyer is a Canadian visual artist and
plant scientist who combines plant materials,
porcupine quills, high-resolution digital tools,
and women's traditional handwork to create
artworks that honour her family's Red River
Métis heritage and recognize plants and
Her fascination with the natural world began
while trekking across the Saskatchewan
prairie with her naturalist mother. This carly
experience grew into a lifelong interest in
healing with herbs and studying plant science.
In 2017, at age 62, she established a studio
practice and began creating a visual language
based on culturally significant plants.
Boyer'swork reflects generational stories
about family, land, and Métis cultural
knowledge. She produces these works using
two techniques she developed: digital beading
and digital quillwork. Recurring motifs reflect
the generational stories she tells
Her work is supported by the Canada Council
for the Arts, the First Peoples Cultural Council,
and the Consell des arts et lettres du Québec.

Colin Brauner's Lab
Colin J. Brauner
Department of Zoology,
Faculty of Science
Below left: Floating research lab in
Tw280090 O0 PEeICU
Physiological adaptations to the environment in fishes
To investigate environmental adaptations (both mechanistic and
evolutionary) in relation to gas-exchange, acid-base balance and ion
regulation in fish, integrating responses from the molecular, cellular and
organismal level. The ultimate goal is to understand how evolutionary
pressures have shaped physiolegical systems among vertebrates and to
determine the degree to which physiological systems can adapt/acclimate
to natural and anthropogenic environmental changes. This information
is crucial for basic biology and understanding the diversity of biological
systems, but much of my research conducted to date can also be applied to
issues of aquaculture, toxicology and water quality criteria development, as
well as fisheries management.
•Gas exchange, haemoglobin and red blcod cell function in fish
• Physiological role of the gills during development and in early
vertebrate evolution
• Patterns of acid-base regulation in fishes and adaptations for air-
breathing in fish
• Optimizing rearing conditions for fish in net-pen and recirculation
aquaculture systems
• Mechanisms resulting in nephrocalcinosus in salmon aquaculture
• Effect of elevated environmental CO2 and elevated temperatures on
fish physiology and conservation
• Effects of elevated total dissolved gases on gas bubble trauma in fish
• Effect of road salt on early life stages of Pacific salmon

image_transcriptions.text:
Aquaculture and Climate Change Lab
Andrea Frommel
Faculty of Land and Food Systems
With the rapid expansion
and intensification of
aquaculture and the
depletion of commercial
fish stocks world-wide, the future of fish is dependent on
sustainable use of this precious resource. In my lab we are
interested in the following main areas:
Effects of climate change on wild commercial populations: We are
researching how synergistic climate stressors
(acidification, warming, hypoxia), and in
particular natural variability, affect vulnerable
early life stages of wild commercial species,
such as Pacific salmon, herring, and sturgeon.
WE WORK:
All across BC.
Mitigating ocean acidification with marine algae: Kelp is an emerging
aquaculture star with uses for direct consumption, health additives.
and feed for livestock. We are looking into the potential of sugar kelp
to mitigate ocean acidification effects on larval fish and shellfish as
well as benefit larval gut microbiota. This has applications for habitat
restoration for wild populations, as well as uses in multi-trophic
aquaculture to improve sustainability and fish welfare.
Sustainable feeds: Feed and medication are one of the largest input
costs for aquaculture operations and the biggest burden on the
environment. In collaboration with industry and the Department of
Fisheries and Oceans, we are researching 1) insect-based feeds as
alternatives to fishmeal for fish that are able to digest chitin and 2)
the uses of humic and fulvic acids as feed additives in hatcheries to
improve immune function.
WEWORK WITH:
Pacific salmon
Arctic char
Sablefish
Pacific herring
Wolf eel
White Sturgeon
UBC

Pacific Salmon Ecology and Conservation
Laboratory
ATUTUNHOaUO
Tehase o chifook salmon
Leettongtt: Katie Zian Stapter
Johinson, and Stott Hnch
Scott Hinch
Department of Forest and
Conservation Sciences
Faculty of Forestry and
Environmental Stewardship
The salmon migration, both as juvenile smolts migrating from natal
freshwater habitats to marine feeding grounds, and as adults returning
to spawning grounds, is among the most remarkable phenomena in
the natural world. Our lab has conducted extensive work to advance
the basic understanding of those migrations and the impact of a range
of environmental conditions that these fish experience on this migration.
This includes investigating the effect of water temperature, salinity.
ocean currents, and river flows that often vary in both space and time.
Climate change has the potential to create new environmental conditions
for migratory salmon to experience. We use a variety of techniques and
tools to create links between the complex environments an individual fish
experiences and its behaviour and survival.
Our work has focused on a range of areas including:
• The physiology of migrations
• Environmental influences on salmon migrations in a changing worid
• Land-use impacts and restoration
• Barriers, fish passage, and olfaction
• Effects of capture and release
• Stress, disease, and pathogens
•Physiology and behaviour of salmon offspring
• Social science and information exchange with stakeholders

image_transcriptions.text:
This exhibit
is supported by
the Wood Family
This tree
grew for
775
years
хреуatр
Thuja plicata
Western redcedar
What can you see in this cross-section through a
775-year-old western redcedar tree? In the 1950s a stump
from BC's coastal old-growth forest was brought to UBC
as a teaching aid, resulting in the affectionate nickname,
"Stumpy". It was exhibited for many years in the center of
the Biological Sciences Building, just north of the Beaty
Biodiversity Museum. This specimen gives us a window
into the ecological, historical, and ethnographic past.
Stumpy
Trees in temperate climates, like ours, grow
a new ring each year. In addition to telling us
how old the tree is, these rings form a record of the
past environment. They can be used to reconstruct
historical climactic conditions from a time before people
starting recording weather. Below is a section cut from
the trunk, but a thin core can be taken from a living tree to
see pattern of rings inside. In spring, when light and water are
abundant, the new cells that form are bigger, have thin cell walls,
and look lighter in colour than the cells grown later in the year.
D

image_transcriptions.text:
DEATY MODIYERSIT
IUSEUN
BENEATH THE EMERALD GREEN WAVES
200 HOURS UNDERWATER IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
The ocean looks cold, deep, and dark from above the surface.
If you are brave enough for a cold dip underwater
wearing an astronaut-like dry suit, you will soon find
a wonderland beneath the emerald green waves
of the Pacific northwest.
In this mysterious underwater world,
height and gravity are no longer barriers.
You can explore the shallow desert-
like barrens in search of Pacific spiny
lumpsuckers hiding on abandoned mooring
lines, or venture deeper to visit a zoanthid
gallery with a giant lingcod. You can play
peek-a-boo with the locals living in sponges
or venture beyond recreational limits in search
of Gorgonian coral reefs. And no matter where
you go, you're free of weight; as if everything is
moving in slow motion until a group of playful sea
lions swiftly dash past you... or you run low on air.
ANTONIO HOU
Antonio Hou is a Master's student at UBC in the Animal Welfare Program at
the Faculty of Land and Food Systems. On land, he spends most of his time
helping animals in shelters find their forever homes and improving their welfare
in kennel environments. In the ocean, Antonio enjoys guiding people at local dive
sites around Metro Vancouver as a divemaster. Since he started cold-water diving
in 2021, Antonio has spent over 200 hours beneath the surface, capturing unique
moments underwater with his camera.
above_thermocline

Female, supermale, or female
impersonator? Some parrotfishes
live in harems with one large male
dominating a group of smaller females.
If this male dies, the largest female
changes sex, size, and colour to become
the new "supermale". Only females that
change sex become "supermales". Fish
that are born male are smaller, but have
one advantage - they look like females.
These sneaky males live among the
females and secretly fertilize their eggs.
1. Japanese parrotfish
Colotomus japonicus
Manazuru, Japan, 1960
No. BC60-0192
2. Loosetooth parrotfish
Nicholsina denticulata
Itabaca Channel, Galapagos Islands, Ecuador, 1956
No. BC56-0434
3. Parrotfish
Cryptotomus sp.
